about: Grading benchmark. Questions, rubrics and answers were written for this project (MIT) about the OpenStax Precalculus fixture pages (CC BY 4.0) listed under each question; the passages sent with each case are those pages as the app chunks them. Expected verdicts follow the rule in docs/tech-plan.md (Tutor): a right answer with a wrong or missing reason is partly correct.

questions.question: Is the relation $\{(1, 4), (2, 5), (1, 6)\}$ a function? Explain why.
questions.referenceAnswer: No. The input 1 is paired with two different outputs, 4 and 6, and a function pairs each input with exactly one output.

criteria.text: States that the relation is not a function
Explains that the input 1 is paired with two different outputs (4 and 6)

questions.question: Find the domain and the range of the function $\{(2, 10), (3, 10), (4, 20), (5, 30), (6, 40)\}$.
questions.referenceAnswer: Domain: $\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ (the first coordinates). Range: $\{10, 20, 30, 40\}$ (the second coordinates).

questions.question: Find the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2}$ and write it in interval notation.
questions.referenceAnswer: The denominator is zero when $x = 2$, so 2 is excluded and every other real number is allowed: $(-\infty, 2) \cup (2, \infty)$.

criteria.text: Excludes $x = 2$ because it makes the denominator zero
Writes the domain in interval notation as $(-\infty, 2) \cup (2, \infty)$

questions.question: What is the domain of $g(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$? Explain your answer.
questions.referenceAnswer: $[3, \infty)$, that is $x \ge 3$: the radicand $x - 3$ must not be negative, because an even root of a negative number is not a real number.

criteria.text: Explains that $x - 3$ (the radicand) cannot be negative for the square root to be a real number

questions.question: Add the matrices $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 5 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.referenceAnswer: Add the entries in the same positions: $A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

criteria.text: Adds the entries in corresponding positions (shown, or evident from a correct result)

questions.question: Explain what multiplying a matrix by a scalar means, then compute $3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.referenceAnswer: Every entry of the matrix is multiplied by the scalar: $3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 0 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$.

criteria.text: Explains that every entry is multiplied by the scalar

cases.question: Q1
cases.answer: No, it is not a function, because the input 1 goes to both 4 and 6.

cases.question: Q1
cases.answer: Not a function: x = 1 shows up with y = 4 and again with y = 6, so one x-value has more than one y-value.

cases.question: Q1
cases.answer: No, because the outputs 4, 5 and 6 are all different numbers.

cases.question: Q1
cases.answer: Yes, it is a function because every pair has an x and a y.

cases.question: Q2
cases.answer: The inputs are the whole numbers 2 through 6, and the outputs are 10, 20, 30 and 40 (10 only counts once).

cases.question: Q3
cases.answer: The denominator is 0 when x = 2, so 2 is left out: (−∞, 2) ∪ (2, ∞).

cases.question: Q3
cases.answer: $x \neq 2$, since $x - 2 = 0$ there and we can't divide by zero; any other real number works. In intervals: $(-\infty, 2) \cup (2, \infty)$.

cases.question: Q3
cases.answer: All real numbers except 2, because x = 2 would mean dividing by zero.

cases.question: Q3
cases.answer: (−∞, 2) ∪ (2, ∞), because x = 2 would make the numerator equal to zero.

cases.question: Q4
cases.answer: [3, ∞), because you can't take the square root of a negative number, so x − 3 has to be at least 0.

cases.question: Q4
cases.answer: x needs to be 3 or bigger. If x were less than 3 then x minus 3 would be negative and the square root wouldn't be a real number.

cases.question: Q4
cases.answer: x ≥ 3, because the square root of 3 is the smallest square root there is.

cases.question: Q4
cases.answer: (3, ∞), since x − 3 can't be negative under a square root.

cases.question: Q4
cases.answer: All real numbers, since you can take the square root of anything.

cases.question: Q5
cases.answer: Each entry of the sum is the sum of the two entries in the same spot: $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

cases.question: Q5
cases.answer: Adding entry by entry gives rows (5, 4), (2, 5) and (−3, 6).

cases.question: Q6
cases.answer: It means you multiply only the entries on the main diagonal by the number. 3 times the matrix is [[3, −6], [0, 12]].

cases.question: Q6
cases.answer: Scalar multiplication adds the number to each entry, so the result is [[4, 1], [3, 7]].
